documents.title: One go-bag for several hazards
documents.body:
Pack one bag the household can carry or load quickly. The same bag is the right start for a flood, a hurricane, a wildfire, or an earthquake, because the first problem is often the same: you may have to leave, or home may be without power and open stores.

For each person, a widely used planning baseline is one gallon of water per day for at least three days, plus food that does not need a stove. Add a flashlight, batteries, a whistle, a phone power bank, a small first-aid kit, and the prescription medicines people in the household actually take. Include copies of identification and insurance, a little cash in small bills, sturdy shoes, and a change of clothes.

If a child, an older adult, or a pet is part of the household, pack what they need specifically. Glasses, hearing aids, and a paper list of phone numbers belong in the bag, because the cell network may not work. Keep the bag by the door you would use to leave. During the months when local hazards are more active, keep the car at least half full.

documents.title: Flood decisions and hurricane decisions
documents.body:
A flood and a hurricane can both require leaving, and both can involve water. The decision is still not the same.

A hurricane often gives a day or more of warning. The dangerous mistake is waiting to see the wind. If your zone is ordered to evacuate, go while roads are still open. Storm surge can flood coastal and tidal areas well before the center of the storm arrives, including places that do not look like a beach. Learn your evacuation zone on a clear day.

A flood can be a river that rises for hours, or a flash flood that arrives in minutes. Leave if officials advise it. Separately, do not drive or walk through floodwater, even on a route you were not using to evacuate. The road underneath may be gone, and the water is often deeper and faster than it looks. If you meet standing water, turn around.

Shared preparation is a go-bag, enough fuel to leave, two ways out of the neighborhood, and a meeting place. The split is this: a hurricane zone order is a reason to leave early. Floodwater on the road is a reason to stop, not to push through.

documents.title: Alerts to join before the season
documents.body:
Join alerts before you need them. Wireless Emergency Alerts are the short official messages a phone can receive for imminent threats. Leave them on. They do not replace a local list.

Also join the system run by your city, county, or parish emergency management office. That list is how many communities send evacuation notices, shelter openings, and boil-water or air-quality messages that a national push will not name street by street. A NOAA Weather Radio is worth having where hurricanes or floods are part of the local risk, because it still works when the internet does not.

Before wildfire season, confirm that the county list is the one that will name your area, and choose an out-of-area contact. Before hurricane season, confirm whether the home is in an evacuation zone and save the official page you will check. Alert systems are a poor thing to learn while you are packing.

documents.title: What to do while the ground is shaking
documents.body:
While the ground is shaking, Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Get down, get under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from glass, and hold on until the shaking stops. Do not run outside during the shaking. Falling brick, glass, and pieces of the building front are a common way people are hurt. A doorway is not a special safe spot.

When the shaking stops, check yourself and the people with you. If you smell gas, or the building is badly damaged, leave then and move to an open area away from walls and wires. Expect aftershocks. Do not use elevators.

This is the opposite of a wildfire evacuation or a hurricane zone order, where the safer move is often to leave before conditions get worse. During shaking, stay and cover. After shaking, leave only if the building is unsafe or officials say so.

documents.title: Wildfire: ready, set, go
documents.body:
Treat wildfire risk as Ready, Set, Go.

Ready, before a fire is anywhere near you: the go-bag is packed, copies of documents are with it, you know the route out, and brush and debris immediately around the home have been reduced where that is your responsibility. Set, when fire weather is high: the bag is at the door, the car has fuel, you have N95 respirators for smoke, and you are watching the local emergency channel. Go means leave early. Waiting until you can see flames often means driving in smoke, in traffic, on the only road out.

If you have not been told to leave, staying inside with windows and doors closed is safer than standing in heavy smoke. An N95 helps for a short trip through smoky air. It is not a reason to ignore an evacuation notice. If you are ordered to leave, leave.

documents.title: A meeting plan that works for every hazard
documents.body:
A plan that works for every hazard is mostly about finding each other.

Pick two meeting places and say them out loud. One should be just outside the home, in case you step out after earthquake shaking or because an alarm is sounding. One should be outside the neighborhood, in case you cannot go back. Choose one out-of-area contact, someone far enough away that the same storm or fire is unlikely to reach them, and agree that everyone will report to that person. Local phone lines get congested. A distant contact often gets through when a neighbor does not.

Write the places and the number on paper, and put a copy in the go-bag. Photograph identification, insurance, and prescriptions and keep those copies with the list. Tell children, roommates, and anyone who is often in the home. You do not need a different reunion plan for a flood, a hurricane, a wildfire, and an earthquake.

documents.title: What to prepare once
documents.body:
A useful plan covers the actions that transfer, then the few decisions that do not.

Do these once for floods, hurricanes, wildfires, and earthquakes. Pack one go-bag and keep it reachable. Leave phone emergency alerts on, and join the local alert list before the season rather than during it. Choose two meeting places and one out-of-area contact. Keep copies of identification, insurance, and a medication list with the bag.

Then learn the split. During earthquake shaking: Drop, Cover, and Hold On, and do not run outside while it is shaking. In a flood: do not walk or drive through water, and leave before routes are cut off if officials advise it. For a hurricane: if your zone is ordered out, leave before wind and surge arrive. For a wildfire: leave early enough that you are not driving through smoke and traffic.

Ask Harbor to go deeper on any one of those. Start with the shared steps, then the decision that belongs to the hazard you actually face.
